100 apps. What can an agent actually build?

I read the official docs for 100 apps across 10 categories to work out where an agent could really build something — and where it can't, and why. Every claim below links to the first-party source I used.

02 / Category matrix

10 categories, six honest outcomes.

“Documented build candidate” means the docs show a real path to build a working prototype. It does not mean I got a production credential.

Patterns

  1. 4/10 categories (40.0% of apps) account for 24/36 production gates (66.7%).
  2. Free/trial self-serve access totals 78 apps for prototypes and 62 for production; 16 apps move behind a production gate. Managed OAuth cannot grant a paid plan, app review, admin approval, or partner access.
  3. 36/100 apps document paid-plan, admin, app-review, or partner access for production.
  4. For 41/80 catalog apps, documented auth is broader than Composio auth_schemes.
  5. 67 apps have hosted-action MCP; local, docs-only, beta, prelaunch, none, and unresolved are distinct.

03 / The research agent

Search is just triage. The evidence is the point.

Official-source discovery → frozen evidence → context-aware extraction → independent review → strict assembly gate.

What my script does

For each app it searches for the API reference, authentication, credential-creation, access/pricing and MCP docs. It saves every raw pass, pulls out the scoped claims, keeps the publication dates, and throws away client-only or negated MCP “proofs” before anything gets assembled.

Where review changed classifications

48 decisions are recorded in the model log: 18 prototype/production splits, 16 MCP tier decisions, and 9 auth-chip decisions, plus 5 other logged reviews. The gold set records 1 fetch-failed excerpt(s). Documented rebrand(s): FanBasis → Commas.

Firecrawl retrieval check

Composio reported an active Firecrawl connection. On a small 6-page illustration (not a benchmark), direct retrieval reproduced 4 stored quotes and Firecrawl reproduced 5. It recovered Pinterest and lost none; all pages returned HTTP 200 in both paths: yes. Lark remains unmatched in both paths despite successful HTTP responses; this may indicate a stored-quote/page-content discrepancy rather than a fetch failure.

Composio SDK cross-check

Composio SDK/catalog listing agreement is 100/100 of 100 apps (80 listed and 20 not listed); this is separate from vendor MCP source verification. For 28 apps with a documented tool count, 15 match the current SDK count; the rest show count drift.

SDK auth_schemes assignments across listed toolkits (one app may have multiple):

  • OAUTH2 — 52 app assignments
  • API_KEY — 44 app assignments
  • S2S_OAUTH2 — 6 app assignments
  • BASIC — 4 app assignments
  • BEARER_TOKEN — 3 app assignments
  • DCR_OAUTH — 3 app assignments

In the 80 apps in the catalog comparison, auth detail agrees on 31; research is broader on 41, Composio on 6, with 1 no-overlap and 1 transport-only cases. This compares documented scope; it is not a wrong-claim count.

04 / Accuracy lab

Coverage first. Then accuracy, with real denominators.

4 labeled fields: coverage rose from 26/80 (32.5%) to 60/80 (75.0%); strict precision fell from 69.2% to 61.7% as more rows were answered; there were 0 incorrect answers. The labels are recorded as produced in a separate AI session; model identity is not recorded, and exclusion of earlier chat labels cannot be verified from saved artifacts. The 6-field score is secondary: it adds catalog matching and rule-derived buildability.

Blind gold · 4 labeled fields

Label provenance: labels are recorded as coming from a separate AI session using frozen page excerpts; the model/session identity was not recorded. The project record says agent answers were not shown during labeling, but the saved artifacts do not establish whether earlier chat labels were excluded; prior-chat blindness is unverified. Gold status across the 80 rows: 60 found, 14 not stated, 6 unresolved. The 1 fetch-failed row (Gladly·credential_gate) and 1 off-topic row (Discord·credential_gate) remain reported. Unresolved rose from 4 to 20: Pass 1 abstained on 50 rows, hiding some unscoreable gold as abstentions. Pass 3 abstained on 0 rows, so all 20 gold-unscoreable rows surfaced. The author's earlier human review matched the gold rating on 58/80 rows (72.5%); this is a same-author spot-check, not independent adjudication. These rows were not newly incorrect. Strict precision is conditional on answered rows; half-credit and its CI use answered rows, while fixed half-credit counts every row with unanswered rows at zero.

Legacy author self-review (not blind gold)

The blind gold panel above is the scored verification. The cards and table below are my own earlier six-field review of the same sample; they are disclosed as self-assessed, not as a blind gold set.

How I checked the accuracy. First my script pulled all six fields for the 60 sampled claims — that is the first pass. Then I went back over the same 60 claims myself: I searched wider, re-read the dates and the surrounding context, and fixed the ones the script got wrong — that is the final pass. I scored both passes over the same 60 claims; unanswered claims score zero.
PassSelected sampleRandom holdoutClaims answered
(selected / holdout)
First pass — script only35.8% (21.5/60)28.3% (17/60)26/60 (43.3%) / 20/60 (33.3%)
After my manual review41.7% (25/60)30.0% (18/60)33/60 (55.0%) / 26/60 (43.3%)

Half-credit means a partly-correct claim counts as 0.5 and an unresolved one counts as 0, out of all 60. My script scored lower on the first pass because its rule insisted on a vendor-root API path, so it gave up on most of the tricky claims. On the claims it did answer it actually looks better — 65.4% against 57.6% on the selected sample — but that is only because my script answered the easy ones and skipped the rest. Once every claim has to count, my review moves the score up: the selected sample goes from 35.8% (21.5/60) to 41.7% (25/60), and the random holdout from 28.3% (17/60) to 30.0% (18/60).

Hits and misses, shown honestly

correct

HubSpot · Vendor MCP

Frozen agent answer: vendor_server

Review: HubSpot's own developer documentation operates the remote MCP server at https://mcp.hubspot.com. It uses OAuth with PKCE, and available tools remain limited by the user's permissions, subscription, and account configuration.

Checked correction: vendor_server: HubSpot-operated remote MCP server at https://mcp.hubspot.com, authorized through OAuth with PKCE and constrained by granted permissions and account capabilities.

partial

HubSpot · Authentication

Frozen agent answer: OAuth 2.0, Bearer token, API key, API token

Review: OAuth, bearer transport, developer API keys, and single-account access tokens are documented, but the list conflates credential types with bearer transport and omits current service keys. Developer API keys are limited to documented app-management endpoints rather than serving as general CRM credentials; service keys entered public beta on February 10, 2026 and replace legacy private apps for new system-to-system integrations.

Checked correction: OAuth 2.0 for distributed apps; static/legacy private-app access token for one authorized account; current account service key for system-to-system access; developer API key only for documented app-management endpoints. OAuth, static tokens, and service keys use bearer authorization.

incorrect

Zendesk · Vendor MCP

Frozen agent answer: client_only

Review: The cited GA announcement proves a Zendesk MCP client, but client support does not prove absence of a vendor server. Zendesk separately documents its own account-specific MCP Server for Bridge/external AI agents in EAP, published October 21, 2026. The server is not GA, but it is a vendor-operated server.

Checked correction: vendor_server_eap: Zendesk operates an account-specific MCP Server for Bridge/external AI agents in EAP, alongside the separate GA MCP client.

06 / Limits and handoff

What this evidence does—and does not—prove.

Documentation, not credentials

I never used a live token, a paid plan, admin approval, a partner agreement or a production connection. If something is gated, that is a real finding, not a failed build.

Dates and absence

Where I could, I kept the page’s published or updated date; when there was none, the field reason says so. “No vendor server documented” only covers the source I cite, and unresolved is not the same as absent.

Security review

The bearer-shaped value in my first Git commit is an exact match for a public Zendesk documentation example. It was not a real user’s credential, so I did not rewrite history or revoke anything.

Next step: start with the documented easy wins, send the gated apps to the exact access step each one needs, and put the partner-only apps into outreach. Recheck the time-sensitive pages before building.
